findings.summary: The code line inside the "Brittle Text Match" callout overflows its box and collides with the right column's code block, overprinting the word "flattened".
findings.evidence: `strings.Contains(err.Error(), "not found")` runs past the callout's green border (box right edge ≈ x531) out to ≈ x578, where the trailing `")` overlaps the glyphs "fl" of "flattened" in the section 5 code block at the same baseline.
findings.fix: Let the callout wrap or shrink long inline code instead of letting it overflow — apply word-wrap/overflow-wrap and a max-width equal to the callout's inner width to the code span in the callout style, or break the sample across two lines after the comma.

findings.summary: The example line in the "String Style" callout overflows the callout box and runs into the page's right margin.
findings.evidence: `openConfig: read /etc/app.conf: denied` extends to ≈ x1034 while the green callout box ends at ≈ x1005 and the page content margin is ≈ x1005; the trailing word "denied" sits on top of and past the box border.
findings.fix: Apply the same wrap/max-width constraint to inline code in callout bullets so the sample wraps inside the box, or shorten the sample to `read /etc/app.conf: denied`.

findings.summary: Page 2 uses the `%w` verb in a worked example (and calls a field "the wrapped cause") two pages before wrapping is defined, with no forward pointer.
findings.evidence: Page 2 code: `return fmt.Errorf("load %q: %w", p, err)` and struct comment `Err error // the wrapped cause`; `%w` is first explained on page 4 ("The %w Verb ... cause kept, not flattened"). The syllabus point carried the pointer "— verb `%w` explained next chapter", which the page drops.
findings.fix: Add a one-line note next to that code block on page 2, e.g. a bullet or inline comment reading "`%w` keeps the cause inspectable — full contract on the next page", and change the struct comment to `Err error // the cause`.

findings.summary: Page 3 prescribes `errors.Is` and behaviour-interface checks as the correct way to compare sentinels, but both — and the wrapping they protect against — are only taught on pages 4–6.
findings.evidence: Page 3: "if errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) {" / "return 404 // survives any wrapping", plus "Behaviour check `interface{ Temporary() bool }` beats identity". `errors.Is` is defined on page 5 ("Reports whether any error in the chain matches `target`"), wrapping on page 4, behaviour matching on page 6 ("An interface target gives behaviour-based matching").
findings.fix: Under the "Compare, Never ==" heading on page 3 add a forward-pointer bullet: "Any layer can wrap this error with `%w` (page 4); `errors.Is` walks the whole chain (page 5) — `==` only sees the outermost error." Likewise tag the behaviour-check bullet with "see `errors.As` (page 6)".

findings.summary: The page claims `io.Copy` and `bufio` return a *wrapped* `io.EOF`, but `io.Copy` never reports `io.EOF` at all and `bufio` returns the sentinel bare.
findings.evidence: "`errors.Is(err, io.EOF)` after `io.Copy` or `bufio` calls" / "Those layers wrap the sentinel rather than return it bare" — but `io.Copy`'s documented contract is "A successful Copy returns err == nil, not err == EOF", and `bufio.Reader.Read`/`ReadString`/`ReadByte` return `io.EOF` itself, unwrapped.
findings.fix: Replace the two bullets with: `io.Copy` swallows EOF and returns `nil`, so never test it for `io.EOF`; `bufio` returns `io.EOF` bare, so `errors.Is` is equivalent to `==` there — use `errors.Is` anyway because *your own* layers (or a decoder) may wrap it later.

findings.summary: Wrong resumption point after `recover`: execution continues in the caller of the function that deferred the recover, not in the caller of the function that panicked.
findings.evidence: "Resumes in the caller of the panicking function, not at the panic site"
findings.fix: Reword to "Resumes in the caller of the function whose deferred call recovered — that function returns immediately; it never continues past the call that panicked." (Handler panics deep, middleware recovers, control returns to the middleware's caller — not into the middleware body.)

findings.summary: The enumeration of the `errors` package is out of date for a 2026 handbook — it omits `ErrUnsupported` (Go 1.21) and the generic `AsType` (Go 1.26).
findings.evidence: "The `errors` package is tiny: New, Is, As, Unwrap, Join"; page 10's "Version Notes" stop at Go 1.20. Current `errors` also exports `ErrUnsupported` (Go 1.21) and `AsType[E error](err error) (E, bool)` (Go 1.26).
findings.fix: List "New, Is, As, AsType, Unwrap, Join" and add to the Version Notes sidebox: "Go 1.21: `errors.ErrUnsupported`" and "Go 1.26: `errors.AsType` — generic, allocation-free alternative to `As`"; mention `AsType` alongside `errors.As` on page 6.

findings.summary: A bullet in section 4 renders with a stranded marker and no text on its own line, and its code content then runs past the column edge.
findings.evidence: A lone "✿" marker sits on one line with nothing after it, and the next line holds `fmt.Errorf("read %s: %v", name, err)` ending at ≈ x1020, past the column right edge of ≈ x1005.
findings.fix: Keep the bullet marker with the first content fragment (no break between marker and content) and allow the long code span to wrap inside the column width rather than pushing wholly to the next line.

findings.summary: The constructor example returns a `ParseError` type that is never declared anywhere in the handbook, while the only struct shown on the page is `PathError`.
findings.evidence: Page 2 declares `type PathError struct { Op, Path string; Err error }` but the constructor block reads `func NewParseError(l int, e error) error {` / `return &ParseError{Line: l, Err: e}`; page 4 then writes `func (e *ParseError) Unwrap() error`.
findings.fix: Make the two examples use one type: either rename the constructor to `NewPathError` returning `&PathError{...}`, or add the two-line `type ParseError struct { Line int; Err error }` declaration above the constructor so page 4's `Unwrap` receiver is defined.

findings.summary: Recommends `interface{ Temporary() bool }` as the preferred behaviour check without noting that `Temporary` has been deprecated since Go 1.18.
findings.evidence: "Behaviour check `interface{ Temporary() bool }` beats identity" (repeated on page 9: "Check `Timeout()`/`Temporary()`-style interfaces via `errors.As`") — `net.Error.Temporary` carries "Deprecated: Temporary errors are not well-defined. Most "temporary" errors are timeouts, and the few exceptions are surprising."
findings.fix: Use `Timeout() bool` or a domain-specific behaviour interface (e.g. `interface{ Retryable() bool }`) as the example, and mark `Temporary()` as deprecated since Go 1.18 on both pages.

findings.summary: The `[recovered]` annotation is attributed to panicking during an unrecovered panic, but the runtime prints it only for a panic that was actually recovered and then re-panicked.
findings.evidence: "Panicking inside a deferred call during a panic prints both" / "Labelled `panic: ... [recovered]` in the output" — `runtime.printpanics` prints `" [recovered]"` only when that `_panic`'s `recovered` flag is set.
findings.fix: Split the claim: a second panic during an unrecovered panic prints `panic: first` then an indented `panic: second`, with no tag; `[recovered]` (or `[recovered, repanicked]`) appears only when the earlier panic was recovered and the deferred function panicked again — the classic `testing` re-panic output.

findings.summary: "`strconv` never panics" is false — the integer formatters panic on an out-of-range base.
findings.evidence: "`strconv` never panics — it returns `*NumError`"; `strconv.FormatInt`/`FormatUint`/`AppendInt` panic with "strconv: illegal AppendInt/FormatInt base" when base < 2 or > 36.
findings.fix: Narrow to the parsers: "`strconv`'s parsers never panic — they return `*NumError`; `FormatInt`/`AppendInt` still panic on an illegal base (programmer error)."

findings.summary: The net/http sidebox implies the stdlib drops the panic silently; the server already logs the panic value plus a full stack trace.
findings.evidence: "Recovers panics per request / Closes the connection / The handler's work is lost anyway / Add your own middleware to log it" — `net/http`'s `conn.serve` recover logs `"http: panic serving %v: %v\n%s"` with a 64 KB stack to `Server.ErrorLog` (skipping only `ErrAbortHandler`).
findings.fix: Change the last bullets to: "Logs `http: panic serving …` plus a stack to `Server.ErrorLog`" and "Sends no response at all — add middleware if you want structured logging and a 500."

findings.summary: Ties the "classic loop-variable trap" to `defer`'s immediate argument evaluation, though that trap is the opposite (late closure capture) and was removed in Go 1.22.
findings.evidence: "Arguments evaluate immediately; the call runs at function exit" / "Classic loop-variable trap lives right there"
findings.fix: Drop the loop-variable bullet or replace it with the trap that actually follows from immediate evaluation — `defer fmt.Println(i)` records `i`'s value at `defer` time — and note that the per-iteration loop-variable change in Go 1.22 killed the old closure-capture version for modules declaring `go 1.22+`.

findings.summary: Page 8 states that converting a panic to an error requires a named return value, but the canonical example omits the enclosing function signature, so the named return is nowhere visible.
findings.evidence: Bullet: "Converting a panic to an error needs a named return value" / "A bare `return` result cannot be reassigned from a defer", next to a code block that starts at `defer func() {` and assigns `err = fmt.Errorf("recovered: %v", r)` with no `func ... (err error)` line.
findings.fix: Wrap the snippet in its signature, e.g. `func Parse(b []byte) (v Node, err error) {` above the `defer func() {` line and a closing `}` below, so the named `err` the defer assigns to is on the page.

findings.summary: The recover-in-a-helper gotcha is filed in the "Debug Kit" sidebox at the end of the page instead of beside the directly-deferred rule it qualifies.
findings.evidence: Page 8 sidebox "Debug Kit" lists "`debug.PrintStack()` inside recover", "`debug.Stack()` to capture it", "The original trace is otherwise lost", then "`recover()` in a helper the defer calls returns nil" — while the rule it belongs to is in the opening section: "Only when called directly inside a deferred function" / "Not directly deferred? Also `nil`".
findings.fix: Move that last item out of "Debug Kit" and into the "Where recover Works" bullet list as a concrete case of the directly-deferred rule (e.g. "A helper the defer calls is not the deferred call — its `recover()` returns nil").

findings.summary: Attributes context cancellation to `errgroup.Group.Wait()` unconditionally, though a plain `errgroup.Group` has no context and the cancel fires on the first error.
findings.evidence: "`errgroup.Group.Wait()` returns the first non-nil error" / "It also cancels the shared context"
findings.fix: Qualify: "With `errgroup.WithContext`, the derived ctx is cancelled the first time a goroutine returns a non-nil error, and again when `Wait` returns; a zero-value `Group` has no context to cancel."
